title: One NaN can leave the rest of the list unsorted
assumption: A NaN in a numeric list just ends up somewhere predictable, and every other value still gets sorted.

input.display: sorted([1, 2, 3, nan]), sorted([nan, 1, 2, 3]) and sorted([3, nan, 1])
input.description: A numeric column (a score, a computed ratio, a percentage with a 0/0 somewhere) that can legitimately contain NaN, sorted for a leaderboard or report.

what_goes_wrong: Where NaN lands depends on where it started ([1, 2, 3, nan] stays as is, [nan, 1, 2, 3] stays as is), and worse, sorted([3, nan, 1]) returns [3, nan, 1]: the numbers 3 and 1 are left out of order. JavaScript's sort with (a, b) => a - b returned [3, NaN, 1] for the same input in Node.js.
why: IEEE 754 makes every ordered comparison with NaN false, so to Python's sort NaN looks equal to everything (neither NaN < x nor x < NaN). In JavaScript, a - b is NaN whenever either side is NaN, and the spec turns a NaN comparator result into 0, which also means "equal". Equality with everything breaks transitivity: 3 "equals" NaN and NaN "equals" 1, but 3 is not equal to 1. Sorting algorithms rely on transitivity to avoid comparing every pair, so they can conclude [3, nan, 1] is already in order. Python's sort makes no promise for inconsistent comparisons, and the ECMAScript spec says the order is implementation-defined when the comparator is not consistent.

repros.code:
nan = float("nan")
print(sorted([1, 2, 3, nan]))
print(sorted([nan, 1, 2, 3]))
print(sorted([3, nan, 1]))

fix: Remove or partition NaN before sorting rather than letting it reach the comparison. Decide whether NaN goes first, last, or is excluded, and encode that directly: in Python, key=lambda x: (math.isnan(x), x) puts NaN last; in JavaScript, a comparator that checks Number.isNaN() on both sides before subtracting.

sources.title: ECMAScript spec: SortIndexedProperties (implementation-defined order for inconsistent comparators)
ECMAScript spec: CompareArrayElements (NaN result treated as +0)
